newsitem.title: CHINA: Cambodia's Sihanouk appeals for mine-clearing aid.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Sihanouk appeals for mine-clearing aid.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk appealed on Wednesday for international aid for clearing mines from his war-shattered homeland.

"As the King of Cambodia, I have the honour to beg humbly for the governments of the richest countries in the world to give direct aid for the de-mining of my unfortunate nation which, at present, is suffering from many terrible ills," he said in a statement issued from his residence in Beijing.
"Among these ills, accidents caused by landmines are the most terrible," he said.

The king, who is in Beijing for medical treatment, said he wanted to pay homage to British mine-clearing expert Christopher Howes who has been missing for months in Cambodia after being kidnapped by "those arch-criminals", the Khmer Rouge.
Cambodia is littered with millions of mines after years of war in the 1960s and 1970s, and the king said as many as 300 Cambodians were wounded or killed each month by mines.

His statement came when Sihanouk was busy meeting international representatives and preparing for talks on Thursday with foreign ministers of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to discuss the crisis in Cambodia after a coup earlier this month.
The king met Yukio Imagawa, a former Japanese ambassador to Cambodia, after Tokyo requested an audience to hear Sihanouk's view on the situation after the coup.
King Sihanouk on Tuesday met Claude Martin, deputy secretary general of the French Foreign Ministry, to discuss the Cambodia crisis but officials refused to give details.
Thai Foreign Minster Prachuab Chaiyasarn and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines arrived in Beijing and Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was due later for talks with Sihanouk on Thursday.
ASEAN has mandated the three foreign ministers to meet Sihanouk to try to promote a negotiated settlement in Cambodia.

Sihanouk, in a letter sent from Beijing on Tuesday to acting head of state Chea Sim in Phnom Penh, called for an end to murder and bloodshed in the conflict between the second prime minister and his son, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who was deposed in the coup.
The king's message followed reports from Phnom Penh quoting Western officials as saying at least 25 people had been killed in custody since Hun Sen seized power in Phnom Penh on July 6.
